section.title: Clean Food and Tithes
section.sectionRationale: This chapter moves from worship centralization and internal loyalty to the visible, everyday markers of Israel's set-apart identity, mourning customs, diet, and generous tithing, showing that holiness was meant to shape the smallest daily habits, not only the great acts of national worship.
section.thesis: As sons of the LORD, a people holy to Him, Israel must mark their identity even in mourning customs and diet, distinguishing clean from unclean creatures, and must give a tenth of their produce both to rejoice before the LORD and, every third year, to provide for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.
section.frameNote: Six movements: sons of the LORD, no pagan mourning rites; clean and unclean land animals; clean and unclean water creatures and birds; no carcasses, and no boiling a young goat in its mother's milk; the yearly tithe eaten joyfully before the LORD; and the triennial tithe for the vulnerable.

units.label: Sons of the LORD: no pagan mourning rites

verses.text: You are sons of the LORD your God; do not cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead,
for you are a people {{qadosh|holy}} to the LORD your God. The LORD has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth.
You must not eat any detestable thing.
These are the animals that you may eat: The ox, the sheep, the goat,
the deer, the gazelle, the roe deer, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the mountain sheep.
You may eat any animal that has a split hoof divided in two and that chews the cud.

But of those that chew the cud or have a completely divided hoof, you are not to eat the following: the camel, the rabbit, or the rock badger. Although they chew the cud, they do not have a divided hoof. They are {{tahor|unclean}} for you,
as well as the pig; though it has a divided hoof, it does not chew the cud. It is unclean for you. You must not eat its meat or touch its carcass.

units.label: Clean and unclean water creatures and birds

verses.text: Of all the creatures that live in the water, you may eat anything with fins and scales,
but you may not eat anything that does not have fins and scales; it is unclean for you.
You may eat any clean bird,
but these you may not eat: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,
the red kite, the falcon, any kind of kite,
any kind of raven,
the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull, any kind of hawk,
the little owl, the great owl, the white owl,
the desert owl, the osprey, the cormorant,
the stork, any kind of heron, the hoopoe, or the bat.
All flying insects are unclean for you; they may not be eaten.
But you may eat any clean bird.

units.label: No carcasses; no boiling a kid in its mother's milk

verses.text: You are not to eat any carcass; you may give it to the foreigner residing within your gates, and he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner. For you are a holy people belonging to the LORD your God. You must not cook a young goat in its mother's milk.

units.label: The yearly tithe eaten before the LORD
units.note: so that you may learn to fear Him

verses.text: You must be sure to set aside a {{ma'aser|tenth}} of all the produce brought forth each year from your fields.

And you are to eat a tenth of your grain, new wine, and oil, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks, in the presence of the LORD your God at the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name, so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always.
But if the distance is too great for you to carry that with which the LORD your God has blessed you, because the place where the LORD your God will choose to put His Name is too far away,
then exchange it for money, take the money in your hand, and go to the place the LORD your God will choose.

Then you may spend the money on anything you desire: cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink, or anything you wish. You are to feast there in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice with your household.
And do not neglect the Levite within your gates, since he has no portion or inheritance among you.

units.label: The triennial tithe for the vulnerable

verses.text: At the end of every three years, bring a tenth of all your produce for that year and lay it up within your gates.

Then the Levite (because he has no portion or inheritance among you), the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied. And the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart. Applied here to a whole people, marking Israel's difference from the surrounding nations even in mourning customs and diet, everyday practices meant to remind them constantly of their unique identity as God's own.

tahor.gloss: Unclean, ritually impure. Describes creatures unfit for Israel to eat, not necessarily because they are inherently evil, but as a divinely established boundary marker teaching Israel to distinguish and discern in every area of life, including the dinner table.

ma'aser.gloss: Tithe, a tenth. A regular, proportionate offering that trained Israel in ongoing worship, joyful dependence on God, and generosity toward the Levite and the vulnerable, rather than a one-time transaction.

basic.context: As sons of the LORD and a people holy to Him, Israel is given specific dietary boundaries and mourning customs that mark them as distinct from surrounding nations, alongside instructions for a yearly tithe eaten joyfully before God and a triennial tithe set aside for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow.
basic.hermeneutics: These specific food laws and mourning customs were covenant markers for Israel's unique identity as a nation, later fulfilled and reinterpreted in the New Testament, which declares all foods clean, Mark 7:19, Acts 10:15. Their abiding principle, that God's people are called to visible, everyday holiness and generosity, carries forward even as the specific dietary boundary lines do not.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is qadosh, holy, set apart, a status marked even in mourning practices and the difference between tahor, clean, and unclean animals at the table. The ma'aser, tithe, was not a one-time tax but a regular rhythm of worship and generosity, both toward God directly and toward the vulnerable in the community.
basic.typology: The clean and unclean distinctions that once marked Israel apart from the nations anticipate the gospel's declaration that God has made all foods, and all peoples, clean through Christ, Acts 10:9-16, 28, dissolving the old dividing wall between Jew and Gentile, Ephesians 2:14.
basic.christ: Peter's vision of clean and unclean animals in Acts 10 directly echoes this chapter's categories, and its meaning, that God has made the Gentiles clean through Christ, breaks down the very distinctions this chapter established, showing how the gospel fulfills and transforms Israel's old boundary markers into a new, worldwide people of God.
basic.god: God delights to be worshiped joyfully, commanding a feast in His presence rather than mere solemn duty, and He is equally concerned for the practical welfare of the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, showing that true worship and practical generosity toward the vulnerable are never separated in His eyes.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 10:9-16, 28 records Peter's vision declaring all foods, and all peoples, clean through Christ. Mark 7:19 records Jesus declaring all foods clean. Ephesians 2:14 says Christ has broken down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile. James 1:27 defines pure religion partly as caring for orphans and widows.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows holiness reaching into the smallest details of daily life, diet, mourning, and giving, training Israel to remember constantly who they belonged to and to care practically for the vulnerable among them. The gospel fulfills this pattern by declaring all foods and all peoples clean in Christ, while carrying forward its call to worship joyfully and give generously to those in need.

context.literary:
The chapter is held together by a frame of identity. It opens, "You are sons of the LORD your God," verse 1, and "you are a people holy to the LORD your God," verse 2, and the same line returns in verse 21, "you are a holy people belonging to the LORD your God." Everything between those two statements, the mourning customs and the whole list of animals, is an explanation of what that identity looks like at a graveside and at a table. The laws do not create Israel's holiness; they express a holiness God has already given.

The food laws are arranged by the realms of creation, land animals in verses 4 to 8, water creatures in verses 9 and 10, and flying creatures in verses 11 to 20, the same order of spheres found in Genesis 1. For land and water Moses gives a test, split hoof and cud, fins and scales. For birds he gives only a list of the forbidden. Unlike Leviticus 11, Deuteronomy names the clean land animals first, ten of them in verses 4 and 5, so that the chapter begins with permission before it turns to prohibition.

The second half of the chapter, verses 22 to 29, turns from what Israel must not eat to what Israel must eat, and where. The tithe is to be consumed "in the presence of the LORD," and the section closes with the vulnerable who "eat and be satisfied," verse 29. So the whole chapter is about eating: what, where, with whom and why.

Within the argument of Deuteronomy, the tithe law begins a run of laws, through 16:17, organised around sacred time: yearly tithes, the third year tithe, the seventh year release, and the annual feasts. Many interpreters read this block as an extended exposition of the Sabbath commandment. The chapter thus stands between the warning against other gods in chapter 13 and that calendar of rest and generosity.
context.historical:
The mourning rites of verse 1 were real and widespread. Israel's neighbours marked grief by gashing the skin and shaving the head, and Scripture records the practice among Moabites, Jeremiah 48:37, and among the prophets of Baal, who "cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom," 1 Kings 18:28. In Canaanite myth even the high god is pictured cutting himself in grief for the dead Baal. Such rites were bound up with ideas about the dead and with fertility gods who died and rose with the seasons. Israel was forbidden them, and so were its priests, Leviticus 21:5. Yet Jeremiah 16:6 and 41:5 show that the customs persisted in Israel long afterward.

The food list reflects the animal life of the southern Levant, though, as the BSB footnote says, the precise identification of some creatures is uncertain. The clean animals are largely the herd, flock and wild game of the hill country. The "rock badger" of verse 7 is probably the hyrax, as the footnote suggests, and like the hare it works its jaws in a way that looks to an observer like chewing the cud. The law describes animals as a herdsman sees them, not in a modern zoologist's categories.

Tithing was an ancient practice. Abram gave a tenth to Melchizedek, Genesis 14:20, and Jacob vowed one at Bethel, Genesis 28:22. Temples and kings across the region collected tithes, and Samuel warned that Israel's king would do the same, 1 Samuel 8:15. Deuteronomy's tithe is strikingly different: the farmer and his household eat much of it themselves at a pilgrimage feast. For those who lived far from the chosen place, verse 25 allows the produce to be sold. The phrase is literally "bind up the silver in your hand," for this was silver weighed and carried in a bundle, not minted coins. The third year tithe stored "within your gates," verse 28, served as a local reserve, a kind of village storehouse for those without land.
context.canonical:
Leviticus 11 gives the fuller version of these laws, including the swarming creatures and the locusts that may be eaten, Leviticus 11:21-22, and it states their purpose plainly: "be holy, because I am holy," Leviticus 11:44-45. Leviticus 20:25-26 ties the distinction between clean and unclean animals directly to Israel's separation from the nations. The distinction itself is older than Sinai, for Noah already took clean and unclean animals into the ark, Genesis 7:2.

Later Scripture shows the laws becoming a test of faithfulness. Daniel refuses to defile himself with the king's food, Daniel 1:8. Ezekiel protests that he has never eaten anything found dead or unclean, Ezekiel 4:14. Isaiah condemns those who eat "the meat of pigs" in pagan rites, Isaiah 65:4 and 66:17. The tithe law is echoed in the third year declaration of Deuteronomy 26:12-15, in Nehemiah's restoration of the Levites' portions, Nehemiah 13:10-12, and in Malachi's charge that Judah was robbing God "in tithes and offerings," Malachi 3:8. Amos mocks worshippers who brought "tithes every three days" while practising injustice, Amos 4:4.

In the New Testament the food laws reach their turning point. Jesus teaches that nothing entering from outside defiles, and Mark adds, "Thus all foods are clean," Mark 7:19. Peter's vision of unclean creatures ends with the word, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean," Acts 10:15, which Peter applies to people, Acts 10:28. Paul says "nothing is unclean in itself," Romans 14:14, that food laws were "a shadow of the things to come," Colossians 2:16-17, and that "every creation of God is good," 1 Timothy 4:4. The identity language of verses 1 and 2 survives intact: believers are "sons of God through faith," Galatians 3:26, and "a people for God's own possession," 1 Peter 2:9. Jesus affirms tithing while rebuking those who neglect "justice, mercy, and faithfulness," Matthew 23:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to understand that belonging to God is not only a matter of great acts at the sanctuary but of ordinary life. The chapter's logic runs from identity to practice: you are His sons, you are holy, you are His prized possession, therefore grieve and eat accordingly. The first hearers were meant to feel the privilege before the restriction.

The mourning law aims at hope. Israel is not to grieve by the rites of peoples whose gods were bound up with death. Their Father is the living God, and so even their sorrow is to be different.

The food laws aim at daily remembrance. Every meal would require a choice that set Israel apart from Canaanite neighbours, and every choice would say, in effect, "we belong to the LORD." Leviticus 20:25-26 makes the connection explicit: the separation of animals mirrors the separation of a people.

The tithe law aims at learning. Verse 23 states its purpose: "so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always." Israel was to learn reverence not by fasting but by feasting in God's presence, acknowledging that every harvest came from Him. The third year tithe aims at justice. The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow are not left to charity at a donor's whim; they have a lawful claim to the harvest, and God attaches His blessing to its faithful payment, verse 29.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter is covenant law for Israel, and different parts of it carry forward in different ways. The food distinctions were given to mark Israel off from the nations, and the New Testament explicitly sets them aside for the church. Jesus declares all foods clean, Mark 7:19, Peter is told not to call unclean what God has cleansed, Acts 10:15, and Paul refuses to let anyone "judge you by what you eat or drink," Colossians 2:16. Believers may therefore eat what Deuteronomy forbade, though Paul asks them to limit that freedom out of love for a weaker brother, Romans 14:20-21.

The principles beneath the rules remain binding. God's people must still grieve with hope, 1 Thessalonians 4:13, still order their ordinary lives, meals included, to His glory, 1 Corinthians 10:31, and still provide for those without means, James 1:27. Whether the tithe itself binds Christians is debated. The New Testament never commands a tenth of the church, but it assumes and exceeds the generosity of the law, calling for cheerful, proportionate and sacrificial giving, 2 Corinthians 9:7, and it keeps the concern for the widow and the stranger at the heart of the church's life, Acts 6:1.

debates.question: Does 'do not cook a young goat in its mother's milk' address a specific pagan ritual practice, and does it establish a broader principle separating meat and dairy?

views.label: A prohibition of a specific Canaanite ritual practice
views.case: Some scholars connected this command to a line in a Ugaritic ritual text that was once read as describing a kid cooked in milk, so that the law would target a pagan fertility rite. The reading of that damaged line is now widely doubted, which weakens this view, although the placement of the command beside the firstfruits in Exodus 23:19 still suggests a setting in worship.

views.label: A humane principle about life and its source
views.case: Others note that Deuteronomy elsewhere forbids taking a mother bird with her young, Deuteronomy 22:6-7, and Leviticus forbids slaughtering an animal on the same day as its young, Leviticus 22:28. On this view it is unfitting to cook a kid in the very milk that was meant to sustain its life. The law trains a sense of reverence for the order of life God made.

views.label: The foundation of the later, broader Jewish practice of separating meat and dairy
views.case: Jewish tradition has long read this command, repeated three times in the Torah, Exodus 23:19, 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21, as establishing the broader kosher principle of not mixing meat and dairy, building a protective fence around the single act named.

debates.bearing: The text itself gives no reason beyond the setting, 'you are a holy people,' verse 21. The humane reading fits the wider patterns of Deuteronomy best, and all three readings agree that the command marked Israel as distinct and taught care in how life is used.

debates.question: Why were some animals clean and others unclean?

views.label: Health and hygiene
views.case: Some have argued that the forbidden animals, especially pigs, scavengers and shellfish, were more likely to carry disease, so that the laws protected Israel's health. The difficulty is that the text never gives this reason, and Jesus' declaration that all foods are clean, Mark 7:19, would be hard to explain if health were the point.

views.label: Symbols of order and wholeness
views.case: The anthropologist Mary Douglas and others proposed that clean animals are those that fit the normal pattern of their realm, land animals that walk on split hooves and chew the cud, fish with fins and scales, while creatures that blur the categories were treated as unclean. The laws thus taught Israel to see holiness as wholeness and order.

views.label: A covenant boundary chosen by God
views.case: Leviticus 20:25-26 links the distinction directly to Israel's separation from the nations. On this view the main purpose was not the nature of the animals but the shaping of a distinct people, which also explains why the boundary could be removed once God began gathering the nations, Acts 10:28.

debates.bearing: The third view rests on the Bible's own explanation and fits the New Testament's handling of the laws. The second may help explain why particular animals fell on each side of the line. The chapter's own frame is identity: 'you are a holy people.'

debates.question: How many tithes did Israel give?

views.label: Several distinct tithes
views.case: Later Jewish tradition distinguished a first tithe for the Levites, Numbers 18:21-24, a second tithe eaten by the worshipper at the sanctuary, Deuteronomy 14:22-26, and a tithe for the poor given in the third and sixth years of each seven year cycle in place of the second, Deuteronomy 14:28-29. This harmonises the laws by treating them as different obligations.

views.label: One tithe described from different angles
views.case: Others think Numbers and Deuteronomy describe the same tenth, which was shared between the worshipper's feast and the Levites in most years and stored for the needy in the third. They note that verse 27 already includes the Levite in the feast.

debates.bearing: The texts do not settle the question. Either way, the tenth was God's, and it served three purposes together: worship, support for those who served at His sanctuary, and justice for those without land.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for "prized possession" in verse 2 is segullah, a king's personal treasure. David uses it of the gold and silver he gave from his own private store for the temple, 1 Chronicles 29:3, and Ecclesiastes 2:8 speaks of "the treasure of kings." God first gives Israel the title at Sinai, "you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations," Exodus 19:5, and Deuteronomy repeats it in 7:6, 14:2 and 26:18. The Greek translators rendered the phrase "a special people," and Paul echoes that phrase when he says Christ gave Himself to purify "a people for His own possession," Titus 2:14.

The verb "cut yourselves" in verse 1 is gadad in its reflexive stem, to gash oneself. It is the verb used when the prophets of Baal "cut themselves with knives and lances," 1 Kings 18:28, and for the mourners of Jeremiah 16:6 and 41:5. The command not to "shave your foreheads" is literally not to make "a baldness between your eyes," a vivid expression for shaving the front of the head.

Verse 3 forbids "any detestable thing," using to'evah, the word translated "abomination" in 13:14. Leviticus 11 describes the same forbidden creatures mainly with a different word, sheqets, "detestable." Deuteronomy's choice of the stronger covenant term links the dinner table with the idolatry of the chapter before: both are things out of keeping with a people who belong to the LORD.

The "carcass" of verse 21 is nevelah, an animal that died of itself rather than being slaughtered, with its blood not drained. Leviticus 17:15 requires anyone, native or foreigner, who eats such meat to wash and be unclean until evening. Deuteronomy allows Israel to give or sell it to the ger, the resident foreigner, who is not under the holiness calling of verse 21. The same ger then appears in verse 29 as a guest at the tithe. He is outside Israel's distinct calling, yet inside its care.

Verse 23 gives the purpose of the tithe with lamad, "so that you may learn." Deuteronomy is a book of learning. The same verb describes Israel gathering at Sinai to "learn to fear Me," Deuteronomy 4:10, the king reading the law so that he may "learn to fear the LORD," 17:19, and the whole assembly, children and foreigners included, hearing the law every seventh year to "learn to fear the LORD," 31:12-13. In chapter 14 the classroom is a feast.

Verse 26 permits "strong drink," shekar, a fermented drink distinct from wine. Priests on duty and Nazirites were forbidden it, Leviticus 10:9, but here it is part of a family's rejoicing before God. The command to "rejoice," samach, is one of Deuteronomy's signatures, running through 12:7, 16:11 and 26:11. And the promise that the vulnerable will "eat and be satisfied," verse 29, uses sava, the word of Deuteronomy 8:10, "when you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God."

typology.type: The dividing line between clean and unclean, verses 3 to 20
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus 20:25-26 says the separation of animals mirrored the separation of Israel from the nations. The New Testament shows the two lines falling together. Jesus declares all foods clean, Mark 7:19, and in Peter's vision the same creatures that Deuteronomy forbade are lowered from heaven with the word, 'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean,' Acts 10:15. Peter grasps the meaning at once: 'I should not call any man impure or unclean,' Acts 10:28. Christ has 'torn down the dividing wall of hostility' to make 'one new man out of the two,' Ephesians 2:14-15. The shadow falls short because it could mark a boundary but never make anyone clean.

typology.type: Sons of the LORD, a holy people, verses 1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: Israel's sonship was corporate and national, Exodus 4:22. In Christ it becomes personal and worldwide: 'You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:26, and the Spirit leads believers to cry 'Abba! Father!', Romans 8:15. Peter transfers the titles of this chapter and Exodus 19 to the church, 'a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' 1 Peter 2:9. Paul brings the two halves of the chapter together, quoting 'Touch no unclean thing' beside 'you will be My sons and daughters,' 2 Corinthians 6:17-18. The escalation is that holiness is now inward, a cleansed heart, rather than a diet.

typology.type: The tithe feast eaten in the presence of the LORD, verses 23 to 26
typology.fulfillment: Israel's families went up to the chosen place to eat and rejoice before God with food and wine from His blessing, and they were told not to forget the Levite. The prophets saw this table widening: 'the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples,' Isaiah 25:6. Jesus says many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Matthew 8:11, and He gives His church a meal of remembrance at which it proclaims His death. The type points to 'the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. It falls short because the tithe feast had to be repeated every year; the final banquet will never end.

typology.type: The third year tithe for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless and widow, verses 28 and 29
typology.fulfillment: The law gave those without land a lawful share in the harvest, stored within the town gates. The early church carried the pattern forward in its daily distribution to widows, Acts 6:1, and James defines pure religion as care for 'orphans and widows in their distress,' James 1:27. Jesus tells His followers to invite to their banquets those who cannot repay, Luke 14:13-14. The escalation is that Christ Himself became poor so that others might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9, and the church gives from that grace. The type falls short because it came only every third year; Christ's people are to give continually.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by its identity statements. Israel is called "sons of the LORD," verse 1, and His "prized possession," verse 2. Jesus is the true Son, the one of whom the Father says, "This is My beloved Son," Matthew 3:17, and through Him those identities are given to all who believe. The New Testament speaks of believers as sons through faith in Him, Galatians 3:26, and of the church as "a people for His own possession," the phrase Paul uses when he says Christ "gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness," Titus 2:14. The treasured people of Deuteronomy 14:2 are purchased and cleansed by His self-giving.

It leads to Christ by the way He handles uncleanness. In the law, contact with a carcass made a person unclean, and holiness had to be protected from contagion. Jesus reverses the direction of the contagion. He touches a man with leprosy and says "Be clean!" Mark 1:41. He touches the coffin of a widow's son at Nain and raises him, Luke 7:14. He eats with tax collectors and sinners, Mark 2:16. Uncleanness does not spread to Him; His holiness spreads to others. That is why He can teach that defilement comes from the heart, not the stomach, and Mark can add, "Thus all foods are clean," Mark 7:19.

It leads to Christ by the gathering of the nations. The clean and unclean lists were a daily reminder that Israel was separated from the peoples. When the gospel went to the Gentiles, God used those same lists in a vision to teach Peter that the separation had ended, Acts 10:15 and 10:28. Paul explains that Christ abolished "in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees" to create "one new man out of the two," Ephesians 2:15. The food laws were a shadow, and "the body that casts it belongs to Christ," Colossians 2:17.

It leads to Christ, too, by the table. The tithe feast was a meal of joy in God's presence, shared with household, Levite and stranger. Jesus' ministry is full of such meals, and He gave the church a meal of its own in which bread and wine proclaim His death until He comes. The widening of Israel's table to the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow anticipates a Messiah whose table is open to the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, Luke 14:13.

Finally, the mourning law finds its ground in Him. Israel was not to grieve like nations whose gods were bound up with death. Christians have a sharper reason: Christ has been raised, so believers "will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope," 1 Thessalonians 4:13. This reading does not turn every animal in the list into a symbol of Christ, which would be forced. The link is the one the New Testament draws: the laws marked a holy people until the Holy One came to make a people holy.
study.god:
The chapter opens by showing God as Father. "You are sons of the LORD your God," verse 1, is not a metaphor chosen at random. God called Israel "My firstborn son" in Egypt, Exodus 4:22, and Moses later asks, "Is He not your Father and Creator?" Deuteronomy 32:6. The food laws and mourning customs are not the demands of a distant ruler but the household rules of a Father who wants His children to reflect His character.

He is the God who chooses. Verse 2 says the LORD "has chosen you," and Deuteronomy 7:7-8 insists He did so not because Israel was great but because He loved them. Holiness therefore begins with God's free choice, not human effort. The command "be holy" always rests on the fact "I have set you apart," Leviticus 20:26.

He is the living God, sharply distinct from the gods of death. Israel's neighbours cut themselves for the dead and for gods who died with the seasons. The LORD is not a god who dies, and He does not want His people's grief to be shaped by despair. The mourning law is a quiet confession that He is Lord of life.

He is the Creator who orders the world. The lists of land, water and sky follow the realms of Genesis 1, and the law invites Israel to see the creatures within a God given order. At the same time, the fact that the New Testament can declare all foods clean shows that uncleanness was never a defect in creation itself. "Every creation of God is good," 1 Timothy 4:4. The distinctions were pedagogical, a teaching tool for a season.

He is the generous Giver who wants to be enjoyed. The tithe was not burned or stored away from the worshipper. God commanded His people to eat it, with "wine, strong drink, or anything you wish," verse 26, and to rejoice. He gives food and wine "that gladdens the heart of man," Psalm 104:15, and He teaches His people to fear Him at a feast. Reverence and joy are not rivals in the presence of this God.

He is the defender of the weak. The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow are named because God Himself "executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing," Deuteronomy 10:18. The third year tithe is one of the ways He does it, through His people. And He attaches a promise, "the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands," verse 29, showing that generosity is not loss in His economy.

For worship, the chapter holds together things we often separate. Holiness and joy, separation and hospitality, reverence and feasting all belong to the worship of the one God. A people who know Him as Father will grieve with hope, eat with gratitude, and open their tables to those who have nothing.

crossReferences.note: The parallel food law in Leviticus ends with the reason behind every distinction: 'be holy, because I am holy.' It ties the diet to the exodus as well, 'I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.' Deuteronomy 14 applies the same holiness to a people about to live in Canaan.

The clearest explanation of the food laws in Scripture. Israel must distinguish clean from unclean animals because God has 'set you apart from the nations to be My own.' The separation of animals is a living picture of the separation of peoples, which is why Acts 10 can treat the two together.

The prophets of Baal 'cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom.' The scene shows exactly the kind of practice Deuteronomy 14:1 forbids, linking self laceration to the worship of Baal and showing why Israel's grief and devotion had to look different.

The third year tithe of 14:28-29 has its own liturgy. The worshipper declares before the LORD that he has given the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless and widow, and asks God to bless Israel and the land. Generosity to the poor is offered as an act of worship with a prayer attached.

Malachi accuses post exilic Judah of robbing God 'in tithes and offerings' and calls them to bring the full tithe into the storehouse. The promise of blessing echoes Deuteronomy 14:29. Neglect of the tithe was not merely stinginess but a breach of covenant with God.

Jesus teaches that what enters from outside cannot defile a person because it does not enter the heart, and Mark comments, 'Thus all foods are clean.' The distinction Deuteronomy 14 drew at the table is ended by the One who locates defilement in the heart.

Peter sees creatures of every kind and hears, 'Get up, Peter, kill and eat!' His protest that he has never eaten anything unclean appeals to laws like Deuteronomy 14. The reply, 'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean,' prepares him to welcome Cornelius, Acts 10:28.

Paul is persuaded 'that nothing is unclean in itself,' yet he urges believers not to destroy a brother over food. The freedom that ends Deuteronomy's food laws is governed by love, and the kingdom of God is 'not a matter of eating and drinking' but of righteousness, peace and joy.

Paul tells believers not to let anyone judge them by what they eat or drink or by feasts and Sabbaths, because these 'are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.' The food laws and the calendar that follows in Deuteronomy 14 to 16 point to Him.

Jesus rebukes scribes and Pharisees who tithed even garden herbs but neglected justice, mercy and faithfulness. He affirms the tithe, 'without neglecting the former,' yet insists on the purpose Deuteronomy 14:29 gave it: care for the vulnerable and a life shaped by God's justice.

Paul quotes 'Touch no unclean thing' and joins it with the promise 'you will be My sons and daughters.' The two ideas that frame Deuteronomy 14, sonship and separation from uncleanness, are applied to the church as a call to moral and spiritual distinctiveness.

James defines pure religion as care for 'orphans and widows in their distress' and keeping oneself unpolluted by the world. It combines the two halves of Deuteronomy 14 in their New Testament form: holiness that avoids defilement, and generosity that feeds the fatherless and the widow.

study.oneStory:
The chapter reaches back to creation. Its lists follow the realms of Genesis 1, land, sea and sky, and it treats food as a gift from the Creator, just as the first command to humanity was about what could be eaten, Genesis 1:29 and 2:16. After the fall, eating itself became the scene of rebellion, and death entered the world. Israel's mourning customs and food laws are given in a world where both death and defilement are real.

God's answer is to form a people. The titles of verses 1 and 2, sons, holy, chosen, treasured, go back to Exodus 19:5-6, where God set Israel apart to be a kingdom of priests among the nations. The food laws kept that calling visible at every meal. The tithes kept it visible at every harvest, as the land's produce flowed back to God, to His servants, and to those without land. Israel's life was meant to show the nations what a redeemed humanity looks like.

The rest of the Old Testament shows the calling kept and broken. Daniel keeps it in Babylon, Daniel 1:8. Nehemiah restores the tithe, Nehemiah 13:12. Malachi exposes a people who rob God, Malachi 3:8. The distinctions that were meant to make Israel a light often became walls of pride instead.

In Christ the story turns. He declares all foods clean, touches the unclean and makes them clean, and through His death tears down the wall between Jew and Gentile, Ephesians 2:14. The treasured people now includes believers from every nation, 1 Peter 2:9. The boundaries of Deuteronomy 14 are fulfilled not by being ignored but by being accomplished: the holiness they pictured is now given by the Spirit to all who believe. The church still grieves with hope and still gives to the poor, but it eats freely and gives thanks, 1 Timothy 4:4-5.

The new creation brings the chapter to its end. The feast before the LORD becomes "the marriage supper of the Lamb," Revelation 19:9. Death, the occasion of the forbidden mourning rites, is gone, and God wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4. Nothing unclean will enter the city, Revelation 21:27, not because the distinctions of the table still apply, but because God's people have been made clean in the blood of the Lamb. The widow, the orphan and the stranger will sit at that table satisfied, and the whole creation will be what the clean animals once pictured: whole, ordered and good.

quiz.q: Why does Moses forbid Israel from cutting themselves or shaving their foreheads for the dead (vv.1-2)?

options.text: Because they are sons of the LORD, a people holy to Him, set apart from pagan mourning customs.
options.note: Verses 1-2 give this exact identity-based reason.

options.text: Because cutting oneself was considered too physically painful.
options.note: Physical pain is not the stated reason; the reason given is Israel's identity as holy to the LORD.

options.text: Because it wasted valuable time during harvest season.
options.note: No such practical concern is mentioned in the text.

options.text: No reason is given for this prohibition.
options.note: Verses 1-2 give an explicit theological reason.

quiz.q: What two characteristics must a land animal have to be considered clean to eat (v.6)?

options.text: A split hoof divided in two, and it must chew the cud.
options.note: Verse 6 states both criteria precisely.

options.text: It must be a domesticated farm animal only.
options.note: Verses 4-5 list both domesticated and wild animals as clean, based on the criteria in verse 6, not domestication status.

options.text: It must be larger than a sheep.
options.note: Size is never mentioned as a criterion in this passage.

options.text: No characteristics are given.
options.note: Verse 6 gives two specific, explicit criteria.

quiz.q: What determines whether a water creature is clean to eat (v.9)?

options.text: It must have fins and scales.
options.note: Verse 9 states this exact criterion.

options.text: It must live only in fresh water.
options.note: No such distinction between fresh and salt water is made; the criterion is fins and scales.

options.text: It must be caught using a net.
options.note: The method of catching is never mentioned as relevant to cleanliness.

options.text: No criteria are given.
options.note: Verse 9 gives an explicit, specific criterion.

quiz.q: What is Israel commanded to do with the yearly tithe of grain, wine, and oil (vv.22-23)?

options.text: Eat it in the presence of the LORD at the place He chooses, so that they may learn to fear Him always.
options.note: Verses 22-23 give this exact instruction and stated purpose.

options.text: Bury it as an offering to the ground.
options.note: No such practice is described; the tithe is to be eaten joyfully, not buried.

options.text: Sell it immediately for maximum profit with no further instruction.
options.note: Verses 24-26 allow converting it to money only when travel distance requires it, and even then it must be spent on a joyful feast before the LORD.

options.text: No instruction regarding this tithe is given.
options.note: Verses 22-27 give detailed instructions.

quiz.q: What happens to the tithe set aside every third year (vv.28-29)?

options.text: It is laid up within the towns so the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow may come and eat and be satisfied.
options.note: Verses 28-29 state this exact purpose and provision.

options.text: It is given entirely to the king's treasury.
options.note: No king or treasury is mentioned; the provision is specifically for the Levite and the vulnerable within the towns.

options.text: It is destroyed completely as a burnt offering.
options.note: The text describes it being eaten by the vulnerable, not destroyed by fire.

options.text: No instruction regarding the third-year tithe is given.
options.note: Verses 28-29 give explicit instruction.

questions: Israel's dietary and mourning customs marked them visibly as 'sons of the LORD,' different from the surrounding nations. What visible, everyday practices in your own life mark you as belonging to God, rather than simply blending in unnoticed?

The yearly tithe was meant to be eaten joyfully in God's presence, teaching ongoing reverence, not merely religious duty. Does your own giving currently feel more like joyful worship or begrudging obligation?

Every third year's tithe provided directly for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, those without their own means of provision. Who are the vulnerable people in your own community that your resources could directly bless this season?

The distinction between clean and unclean foods gave Israel a constant, daily reminder of their set-apart identity, even at the dinner table. What ordinary, daily moment in your own life could become a deliberate reminder of your identity in Christ?

Moses ties tithing to learning 'to fear the LORD your God always' (v.23). How might regular, generous giving actually be shaping your own reverence for God, rather than merely funding causes you support?

translationNotes.note: Cutting oneself and shaving the forehead for the dead were known Canaanite mourning practices; Israel's prohibition visibly distinguished their hope in the living God from surrounding pagan grief rituals.

'Do not cook a young goat in its mother's milk' may address a specific Canaanite ritual practice, and this same command, repeated three times in the Torah, later became the foundation for the broader Jewish practice of separating meat and dairy.
The stated purpose of the tithe, 'that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always,' frames tithing as a tool for ongoing spiritual formation, not merely a financial obligation.
